paragraphs.title: Destruction and the Absence of Salvation

answers: To the enemy
To God
To the prophet
easy.explanation: The psalm begins, “O God, why hast thou cast us off for ever?”
easy.q: To whom does the psalmist speak at the beginning of the passage?

answers: The people God purchased and redeemed
The enemies of Israel
The rivers of the land
easy.explanation: God’s congregation is described as the inheritance He purchased and redeemed.
easy.q: What does God’s congregation represent in verse 2?

answers: They rebuilt it
They decorated it
They cast fire into it and defiled it
easy.explanation: The KJV says, “They have cast fire into thy sanctuary” and defiled the dwelling place of God’s name.
easy.q: What did the enemies do to God’s sanctuary?

answers: They were destroyed and burned
They remained completely safe
They were moved to another land
medium.explanation: The sanctuary and the synagogues of God in the land were burned and brought down.
medium.q: How does the passage describe the condition of the holy places?

answers: Their ensigns for signs
Altars for worship
Tents for the poor
medium.explanation: Verse 4 says, “they set up their ensigns for signs” in the midst of God’s congregations.
medium.q: What did the enemies raise among the congregations?

answers: There was no one to tell them how long the suffering would last
It showed that the enemy had fled
It explained how the seasons changed
medium.explanation: The people said, “We see not our signs,” and had no prophet or person who knew how long the trouble would continue.
medium.q: Why is the absence of signs and prophets significant?

answers: The destruction causes him to question why God has rejected His people and remains inactive
The destruction proves that Israel has won
The destruction explains the origin of day and night
challenge.explanation: The ruined sanctuary leads the psalmist to ask why God has cast His people off and withdrawn His hand.
challenge.q: What connection does the psalmist make between the destruction of the sanctuary and his opening question?

answers: Confidence that the enemy will leave immediately
A sense of devastation, helplessness, and absent deliverance
Joy over the rebuilding of the sanctuary
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from rejection and ruin to the loss of signs, prophets, and hope for an end to the suffering.

answers: Stop withdrawing His hand and act
Ask the enemy to rebuild the sanctuary
Explain the changing seasons
challenge.explanation: The question, “Why withdrawest thou thy hand?” is a call for God to take His hand out of His bosom and act.
challenge.q: What does the psalmist ask God to do near the end of the passage?

paragraphs.title: God’s Power in Creation and the Past

answers: As his King of old
As a new prophet
As a sea creature
easy.explanation: Verse 12 says, “For God is my King of old, working salvation in the midst of the earth.”
easy.q: How does the psalmist describe God at the beginning of this passage?

answers: He prepared only the light
He broke the heads of dragons and Leviathan
He established only the borders of the earth
easy.explanation: The psalmist recalls that God divided the sea and broke the heads of the dragons and Leviathan.
easy.q: What did God do in the sea according to the passage?

answers: The light and the sun
The enemies’ ensigns
The synagogues of the land
easy.explanation: The verse says, “thou hast prepared the light and the sun.”
easy.q: What did God prepare according to verse 16?

answers: He created winter, set borders, and made the sun
He divided the sea, broke the sea monsters, and dried up mighty rivers
He raised the enemies’ banners, burned the sanctuary, and hid the prophets
medium.explanation: The passage describes God’s power over the sea, its creatures, fountains, and rivers.
medium.q: Which sequence best describes God’s works in the waters?

answers: Powerful or great streams of water
Holy places of worship
Messages from prophets
medium.explanation: The phrase appears in the description of God drying up the waters.
medium.q: What does the phrase “mighty rivers” refer to in context?

answers: It mentions day and night, the borders of the earth, summer, and winter
It mentions only the sanctuary
It mentions only the enemy’s army
medium.explanation: The psalmist describes God’s authority over the daily cycle, the earth’s boundaries, and the seasons.
medium.q: How does the passage present God’s rule over time and space?

answers: It reminds him that God has acted powerfully and brought salvation before
It proves that God has no connection with the earth
It shows that God is weak before His enemies
challenge.explanation: Remembering God’s mighty acts gives a foundation for asking Him to act again.
challenge.q: Why might recalling God’s past works strengthen the psalmist’s request for help?

answers: They are all presented as realms under God’s control
They are all described as enemies of Israel
They are all connected with the absence of prophets
challenge.explanation: The passage expands the description of God’s power from the waters to the order of the world.
challenge.q: What common idea connects the sea, rivers, day, and seasons?

answers: God’s ancient and continuing rule and saving work
That God began acting only at that moment
That the enemies were greater than God
challenge.explanation: The title presents God as the psalmist’s longstanding King who has worked salvation from ancient times.
challenge.q: What does the expression “my King of old” emphasize?

paragraphs.title: A Plea to Remember the Covenant and Protect the Vulnerable

answers: The enemy’s reproach and the foolish people who blasphemed His name
The changing seasons only
The heads of Leviathan
easy.explanation: The psalmist asks God to remember how the enemy reproached Him and how the foolish people blasphemed His name.
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask God to remember?

answers: The poor and needy
The enemies alone
The mighty rivers
easy.explanation: He asks God not to forget “the congregation of thy poor for ever.”
easy.q: Whom does the psalmist ask God not to forget?

answers: The covenant
The borders of the earth
The enemies’ signs
easy.explanation: Verse 20 says, “Have respect unto the covenant.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask God to regard?

answers: The covenant gives a basis for asking God to protect His people
The covenant explains the changing of day and night
The covenant describes how rivers were formed
medium.explanation: By appealing to the covenant, the psalmist asks God not to abandon His people amid cruelty.
medium.q: What is the connection between the covenant and the request for deliverance?

answers: Places filled with violence and oppression
Signs seen in the heavens
Weapons used by the enemy
medium.explanation: The phrase describes the dark places of the earth as dwellings where cruelty is found.
medium.q: What does “the habitations of cruelty” describe?

answers: That they return ashamed
That they lose sight of the sun
That they leave the earth
medium.explanation: Verse 21 says, “O let not the oppressed return ashamed.”
medium.q: What does the psalmist ask not to happen to the oppressed?

answers: To present the dishonor done to God and the oppression of the weak as reasons for God to act
To replace the plea for help with a description of creation
To prove that the poor are the enemies
challenge.explanation: The passage joins concern for God’s name with concern for the oppressed and needy.
challenge.q: Why does the psalmist mention both the enemies’ blasphemy and the people’s suffering?

answers: The psalmist moves from mentioning the enemy to asking God to protect His vulnerable people
He moves from night to summer
He moves from rivers to sea monsters
challenge.explanation: After recalling the enemy’s reproach, he asks God to preserve the poor and oppressed.
challenge.q: What change in thought occurs in these verses?

answers: Hope that they will be delivered and no longer disgraced
A request that they join the enemy
A claim that they do not need help
challenge.explanation: Their praise implies the hope that God will rescue them from shame and oppression.
challenge.q: What may be expressed by the request that the poor and needy praise God’s name?

paragraphs.title: A Call for God to Plead His Own Cause

answers: Arise and plead His own cause
Hide from the enemy
Create the seasons
easy.explanation: The psalmist says, “Arise, O God, plead thine own cause.”
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask God to do?

answers: The foolish man’s
The poor man’s
The prophet’s
easy.explanation: The verse asks God to remember how “the foolish man reproacheth thee daily.”
easy.q: Whose reproach does the psalmist ask God to remember?

answers: The voice of His enemies and their continuing tumult
Summer and winter
The fountains and rivers
easy.explanation: The final verse says, “Forget not the voice of thine enemies,” whose tumult increases continually.
easy.q: What does the psalmist ask God not to forget?

answers: Because the enemy has reproached and blasphemed His name as well as harmed His people
Because day and night have changed places
Because the rivers dried up by themselves
medium.explanation: The appeal shows that the conflict concerns both the suffering of the people and the dishonor done to God.
medium.q: Why is God called upon to plead His own cause?

answers: Loud noise and disorder
A covenant
A deliverance
medium.explanation: “Tumult” describes the loud and disorderly uproar of those who rise against God.
medium.q: What does “tumult” mean in this context?

answers: It continues and does not cease
It was heard only once
It disappeared immediately
medium.explanation: The word emphasizes that the enemies’ uproar keeps increasing without stopping.
medium.q: What does the word “continually” show about the enemies’ voice?

answers: It turns the descriptions and pleas into a direct call for God to act
It changes entirely to a description of the seasons
It cancels the request to protect the people
challenge.explanation: After describing the enemy and the suffering, the psalmist directly calls God to arise and respond.
challenge.q: How does the ending continue the psalmist’s earlier requests?

answers: God’s defense of His name and His response to His enemies
An explanation of the sea monsters
A description of the earth’s borders
challenge.explanation: The psalmist asks God to plead His own cause and remember the enemies who oppose Him.
challenge.q: What is the main focus of the final appeal?

answers: God is called to arise and act, while the enemy’s uproar continues to increase
God is described as shouting, while the enemy is silent
God is described as a sea monster, while the enemy is poor
challenge.explanation: The appeal for God to arise is set against the continuing tumult of those who rise against Him.
challenge.q: What contrast appears between God and the enemy in these verses?
